_about: Hand-written key points for pyt-physiology.html (27 Nov 2026, lead). Samples: FMGE recalls, no images.
subject: Physiology
intro: Physiology in FMGE tests mechanisms you can reason out once you know them: the cardiac cycle, the nephron, the oxygen curve, nerve conduction and hormone control. These are the topics that keep coming back, most-asked first, with the one thing to remember about each.

phy.cvs.cycle.note: S1 = closure of mitral and tricuspid valves, at the start of isovolumetric contraction. S2 = closure of aortic and pulmonary valves, at the start of isovolumetric relaxation. S3 = rapid ventricular filling (normal in the young, heart failure in adults). S4 = atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle. Splitting of S2 widens on inspiration.
phy.cvs.cycle.why: S2 is the closure of the semilunar valves, which starts isovolumetric relaxation.

phy.cvs.co.note: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume (about 5 L/min). Measured by the Fick principle or thermodilution. Venous return is driven by mean systemic filling pressure minus right atrial pressure; over time output equals venous return.
phy.cvs.co.why: Venous return depends on the gradient from mean systemic filling pressure to the right atrium.

phy.cvs.fs.note: Frank-Starling law: the more the ventricle is filled (preload, end-diastolic volume), the stronger the next contraction, up to a limit. Bleeding lowers preload, so stroke volume and output fall. Contractility (inotropy) shifts the whole curve.
phy.cvs.fs.why: Blood loss lowers venous return and preload, so stroke volume and cardiac output fall.

phy.cvs.pv.note: The pressure-volume loop: width = stroke volume; area = stroke work. More preload widens the loop to the right; more afterload makes it taller and narrower; more contractility moves the end-systolic point up and left. Aortic stenosis: high peak pressure; mitral regurgitation: no true isovolumetric phases.

phy.cvs.ecg.note: P wave: atrial depolarisation. PR interval: AV node delay (0.12-0.20 s). QRS: ventricular depolarisation. T wave: ventricular repolarisation. The plateau (phase 2) of the ventricular action potential comes from calcium entering through L-type channels; SA node pacemaker potential comes from funny (If) sodium current.
phy.cvs.ecg.why: Calcium influx through L-type channels holds the plateau, phase 2.

phy.cvs.hemo.note: Flow = pressure difference ÷ resistance. Poiseuille: resistance rises with the 4th power of a falling radius, so arterioles control resistance. Basal arteriolar tone is mainly sympathetic (α1). Laminar flow is silent; turbulence (high Reynolds number) causes murmurs and bruits.
phy.cvs.hemo.why: Resting arteriolar tone is kept up mainly by sympathetic vasoconstrictor nerves.

phy.resp.vol.note: Tidal volume about 500 mL; residual volume about 1.2 L (cannot be measured by spirometry; use helium dilution or body plethysmography). FRC = ERV + RV, where the lung's inward recoil balances the chest wall's outward recoil. Vital capacity = IRV + TV + ERV.
phy.resp.vol.why: FRC is the volume where the inward pull of the lung equals the outward spring of the chest wall.

phy.resp.pft.note: Obstructive disease: low FEV1/FVC, high TLC and RV (air trapping, auto-PEEP from incomplete emptying). Restrictive: normal or high FEV1/FVC, low TLC. DLCO falls in emphysema and fibrosis. Peak flow tracks asthma.
phy.resp.pft.why: Narrowed airways do not let the lungs empty before the next breath, so air is trapped (auto-PEEP).

phy.resp.gas.note: V/Q is highest at the lung apex and lowest at the base. Dead space (ventilated, not perfused): pulmonary embolism raises it. Shunt (perfused, not ventilated): does not improve with oxygen. Diffusion follows Fick's law; CO2 diffuses about 20 times faster than O2.
phy.resp.gas.why: An embolus stops blood flow to ventilated alveoli, so physiological dead space rises.

phy.resp.o2.note: Right shift (oxygen given up more easily): high CO2, acid, heat, 2,3-BPG, exercise. Left shift: fetal haemoglobin, carbon monoxide, alkalosis, cold, low 2,3-BPG. P50 is about 27 mmHg. Most CO2 travels as bicarbonate (about 70%), the rest on haemoglobin and dissolved.
phy.resp.o2.why: Fetal haemoglobin binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so it holds oxygen tighter: a left shift.

phy.resp.reg.note: Central chemoreceptors (medulla) respond to CO2 through CSF pH: the main drive. Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid, aortic bodies) respond mainly to low PO2. The fast rise in breathing at the start of exercise is neural (central command and limb receptors); chemical changes come later.
phy.resp.reg.why: Breathing rises at once when exercise starts, before blood gases change: a neural signal.

phy.ren.gfr.note: GFR is about 125 mL/min, best measured by inulin clearance (creatinine in practice). Constricting the afferent arteriole lowers GFR; constricting the efferent raises it (angiotensin II does this). Autoregulation: myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback (macula densa).

phy.ren.cl.note: Clearance = urine concentration × urine flow ÷ plasma concentration. Inulin clearance = GFR. PAH clearance = renal plasma flow (about 625 mL/min) and is the highest, since PAH is filtered and secreted. Glucose clearance is normally zero.
phy.ren.cl.why: PAH is filtered and secreted almost completely, so its clearance is the highest.

phy.ren.tub.note: The proximal tubule reabsorbs about 65% of sodium and water, all glucose and amino acids. The thick ascending limb is impermeable to water (Na-K-2Cl pump; loop diuretics act here). Distal tubule: thiazides; collecting duct: ADH (aquaporin-2) and aldosterone.
phy.ren.tub.why: The ascending limb of the loop of Henle pumps salt out but lets no water follow.

phy.ren.conc.note: The loop of Henle is the countercurrent multiplier; the vasa recta are the countercurrent exchanger. Urea recycling adds to medullary concentration. Maximum urine concentration about 1,200-1,400 mOsm/kg; ADH decides how much water the collecting duct takes back.
phy.ren.conc.why: The loop of Henle builds the medullary concentration gradient: it is the countercurrent multiplier.

phy.ren.ab.note: Bicarbonate is the most important buffer outside cells; haemoglobin is the main buffer of CO2 in blood; phosphate and proteins work inside cells. The kidney adds new bicarbonate by excreting H+ as ammonium and titratable acid. Normal pH 7.35-7.45, bicarbonate 22-26, PaCO2 35-45.
phy.ren.ab.why: The bicarbonate system is the main extracellular buffer because both its parts are regulated (lungs and kidneys).

phy.endo.pit.note: Anterior pituitary: GH, prolactin, ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH. Posterior (made in the hypothalamus): ADH and oxytocin. Prolactin is held down by dopamine. GH rises in deep sleep, fasting and stress. ACTH drives cortisol's daily rhythm (peak early morning).
phy.endo.pit.why: The circadian rhythm of cortisol follows the rhythm of ACTH release.

phy.endo.thy.note: T4 is made more, T3 is the active form (converted in tissues by deiodinase). Iodide trapping (sodium-iodide symporter), organification by thyroid peroxidase, coupling. Thyroid hormone is the main controller of basal metabolic rate. TSH is the best single test of thyroid status.
phy.endo.thy.why: Thyroid hormones set the basal metabolic rate by raising cellular oxygen use.

phy.endo.adr.note: Zona glomerulosa: aldosterone (salt). Fasciculata: cortisol (sugar). Reticularis: androgens (sex). Medulla: adrenaline and noradrenaline. Cortisol from the fetus matures the lungs (surfactant); that is why mothers get steroids before preterm birth.
phy.endo.adr.why: Cortisol stimulates surfactant production by type II cells in the fetal lung.

phy.endo.panc.note: β cells make insulin (with C-peptide), α cells glucagon, δ cells somatostatin. Insulin moves glucose into muscle and fat through GLUT4. Oral glucose releases more insulin than IV glucose because of incretins (GLP-1, GIP).
phy.endo.panc.why: Insulin moves glucose into skeletal muscle after a meal through GLUT4.

phy.endo.ca.note: PTH raises calcium: bone resorption, kidney reabsorption, and more activation of vitamin D (1α-hydroxylase). Calcitriol increases gut absorption. Calcitonin lowers calcium (minor role). Low magnesium blocks PTH release.
phy.endo.ca.why: Parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium partly by increasing bone resorption.

phy.neuro.neuron.note: Resting membrane potential (about −70 mV) is set mainly by potassium leak. Depolarisation: sodium in; repolarisation: potassium out. Conduction is faster in thicker, myelinated fibres (saltatory, at nodes of Ranvier). Fastest: Aα fibres; slowest: C fibres (unmyelinated).
phy.neuro.neuron.why: In myelinated fibres conduction speed rises with fibre diameter.

phy.neuro.syn.note: Main excitatory transmitter in the brain: glutamate; main inhibitory: GABA (spinal cord also glycine). Neuromuscular junction: acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors. Synaptic delay about 0.5 ms; fatigue at synapses is from transmitter depletion.
phy.neuro.syn.why: GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter in the adult brain.

phy.neuro.sens.note: Dorsal column (medial lemniscus): fine touch, vibration, position; crosses in the medulla. Spinothalamic: pain and temperature; crosses in the cord near entry. Utricle and saccule sense linear acceleration and head position; semicircular canals sense rotation.
phy.neuro.sens.why: The utricle and saccule detect linear acceleration and gravity; the canals detect rotation.

phy.neuro.motor.note: Upper motor neurone lesion: spasticity, brisk reflexes, upgoing plantar (Babinski), no wasting early. Lower motor neurone: flaccid, wasting, fasciculations, absent reflexes. The muscle spindle senses stretch (stretch reflex); the Golgi tendon organ senses tension (inverse stretch reflex).
phy.neuro.motor.why: The muscle spindle senses stretch and drives the stretch (knee-jerk) reflex.

phy.neuro.bg.note: Basal ganglia plan and smooth movement. Direct pathway (D1) eases movement; indirect (D2) suppresses it. Loss of nigral dopamine = Parkinson (hypokinetic). Caudate damage = Huntington chorea; subthalamic nucleus lesion = hemiballismus on the other side.

phy.neuro.cbl.note: The cerebellum coordinates movement on the same side. Signs: intention tremor, dysmetria (past-pointing), dysdiadochokinesia, ataxic gait, nystagmus, scanning speech, low tone. Vermis lesions affect the trunk; hemisphere lesions the limbs.
phy.neuro.cbl.why: A cerebellar hemisphere lesion causes intention tremor and dysmetria on the same side.

phy.haem.rbc.note: Erythropoietin is made by kidney peritubular cells when hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) rises. Red cell life about 120 days; destroyed in the spleen. Iron is absorbed in the duodenum (ferrous form) and controlled by hepcidin.
phy.haem.rbc.why: Hypoxia stabilises HIF, which switches on the erythropoietin gene.

phy.haem.hemo.note: Steps: vasoconstriction, platelet plug (adhesion through von Willebrand factor and GPIb, aggregation through GPIIb/IIIa), coagulation cascade, then fibrinolysis by plasmin. Vitamin K-dependent factors: II, VII, IX, X (and proteins C and S).

phy.haem.bg.note: ABO antibodies are naturally IgM. O negative: universal red cell donor; AB positive: universal recipient. Bombay blood group (Oh) has no H antigen, so it reacts with all ordinary blood including O; only Bombay blood can be given. Rh antibodies are IgG and cross the placenta.
phy.haem.bg.why: Bombay (Oh) people make anti-H, so only Bombay (Oh) blood is safe for them.

phy.gi.gast.note: Phases: cephalic (vagus, about 30%), gastric (gastrin, the biggest), intestinal. Parietal cells make acid and intrinsic factor; chief cells pepsinogen; G cells gastrin. Histamine, acetylcholine and gastrin all stimulate acid; somatostatin inhibits it.
phy.gi.gast.why: The gastric phase, driven by gastrin from food in the stomach, makes most of the acid.

phy.gi.panc.note: Secretin (from duodenal S cells, triggered by acid) brings bicarbonate-rich fluid. Cholecystokinin (I cells, triggered by fat and protein) brings enzymes and contracts the gallbladder. Trypsinogen is activated by enterokinase.

phy.gi.bile.note: Bile acids are made from cholesterol; about 95% are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum (enterohepatic circulation). CCK contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi. Ileal disease or resection leads to fat malabsorption and gallstones.

phy.gi.mot.note: Liquids leave the stomach according to volume (pressure gradient); solids more slowly; fat slows emptying most (CCK). The migrating motor complex sweeps the fasting gut (motilin). Peristalsis is coordinated by the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus.
phy.gi.mot.why: Liquid emptying is driven by the pressure from the volume in the stomach.

phy.repro.mens.note: Follicular phase: FSH grows the follicle, oestrogen rises; rising oestrogen switches to positive feedback and causes the LH surge, and ovulation follows about 36 hours later. Luteal phase (fixed about 14 days): progesterone from the corpus luteum, which raises body temperature.
phy.repro.mens.why: Progesterone raises basal body temperature after ovulation.

phy.repro.sperm.note: FSH acts on Sertoli cells (spermatogenesis, inhibin); LH acts on Leydig cells (testosterone). Spermatogenesis takes about 64-74 days and needs a scrotal temperature 2 °C below body temperature. Outside testosterone suppresses GnRH, LH and FSH, so the testes shrink and sperm counts fall.
phy.repro.sperm.why: Injected testosterone feeds back to lower GnRH, LH and FSH.

phy.repro.preg.note: hCG keeps the corpus luteum going until the placenta takes over progesterone production (about 8-10 weeks); it peaks around 10 weeks. Human placental lactogen raises maternal blood sugar (insulin resistance). Relaxin softens ligaments.

phy.repro.lact.note: Prolactin makes milk; oxytocin ejects it (let-down reflex from suckling). High oestrogen and progesterone in pregnancy block milk production; their fall after delivery lets it start. Suckling also suppresses ovulation (lactational amenorrhoea).
phy.repro.lact.why: Oxytocin contracts the myoepithelial cells, ejecting milk; prolactin only makes it.

phy.gen.mem.note: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion (carriers, channels), primary active transport (Na-K ATPase: 3 Na out, 2 K in), secondary active transport (SGLT, Na-glucose co-transport). Cystic fibrosis: the CFTR chloride channel is faulty.
phy.gen.mem.why: CFTR is a chloride channel; its defect causes cystic fibrosis.

phy.gen.pot.note: The resting potential lies close to potassium's equilibrium potential because the resting membrane is most permeable to potassium. Nernst equation gives one ion's potential; Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz combines several. High blood potassium makes the resting potential less negative.
phy.gen.pot.why: Potassium permeability is highest at rest, so it sets the resting potential.

phy.gen.rec.note: G-protein receptors use second messengers (cAMP, IP3 and DAG, calcium). Receptor tyrosine kinases: insulin, growth factors. Nuclear receptors act as transcription factors: steroids, thyroid hormone, vitamin D, retinoids. Ion channel receptors: nicotinic, GABA-A.
phy.gen.rec.why: Nuclear (intracellular) receptors bind the hormone and then bind DNA to switch genes on or off.

phy.mus.sk.note: Calcium binds troponin C, moving tropomyosin off actin's binding sites. ATP is needed to release myosin from actin (no ATP = rigor mortis). Force is greatest at the optimum sarcomere length where actin and myosin overlap best. Smooth muscle uses calmodulin instead of troponin.
phy.mus.sk.why: In smooth muscle calcium binds calmodulin (there is no troponin).

phy.mus.card.note: Cardiac muscle cannot be tetanised because of its long refractory period. Cells are joined by intercalated discs with gap junctions (a functional syncytium). Calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Strength rises with stretch (Frank-Starling).

phy.hmf.title: Higher mental functions: memory, speech, sleep
phy.hmf.note: Broca area (inferior frontal): expressive aphasia; Wernicke (superior temporal): receptive aphasia. Hippocampus: forming new memories (damaged in Alzheimer, Korsakoff). REM sleep: dreams, low muscle tone; deep sleep (N3): delta waves, GH release. EEG alpha waves: awake, eyes closed.
